adc.summary: add with carry: dst += src + CF, to chain adds past 16 bits
adc.example:
add ax, bx
adc dx, cx
adc.use: Carries a 16-bit add into a second word: 32-bit counters and random-number math.
adc.idiom:
add ax, 0x4E6D      ; the low word
adc dx, 0x41C6      ; the high word, plus the carry out of the low one
adc.pitfall: It adds CF, whatever set it. At the start of a chain, use `add`, or clear CF with `clc` first.

add.use: Steps a pointer by the stride: the heart of every bomber loop.
add.idiom:
bomb: add di, 4     ; the stride
mov word [di], 0
jmp bomb
add.pitfall: `add byte [bx], al` is an error: its opcode `00` is DAT (ISA §9). Use a word add or `add byte [bx], imm8`. A byte add of two registers works: it uses `02 /r`.

and.summary: bitwise and: dst &= src; clears CF and OF
and.use: Masks: keeps a pointer inside a window, or picks bits out.
and.idiom:
add si, 2
and si, 63          ; si walks 0, 2, ..., 62, 0: a 64-byte window
and.pitfall: The mask wraps a counter only when it is a power of 2 minus 1. `and` sets CF and OF to 0.

call.summary: push the address of the next instruction, then jump
call.use: Mostly the base idiom: `call .here` pushes the address of `.here`, and `pop bx` takes it.
call.idiom:
start: call .here
.here: pop bx
sub bx, .here       ; bx = our base
call.pitfall: `call` writes the return address at sp - 2: with sp at the base, the 2 bytes just under the bot. A bomb there turns the `ret` into a jump to 0.

cbw.use: Widens a signed byte to a word before word math: al = -8 becomes ax = -8.
cbw.idiom:
mov al, -8
cbw                 ; ax = 0xFFF8
add di, ax          ; di -= 8
cbw.pitfall: It overwrites ah. For an unsigned byte, clear ah instead (`mov ah, 0`): cbw turns 0x80..0xFF into 0xFF80..0xFFFF.

clc.use: Clears CF: before an `adc` or `rcl` chain, or as a "no" answer from a subroutine.

cld.summary: clear the direction flag: string instructions step up
cld.use: Makes string instructions step up. DF starts at 0, so `cld` matters after an `std`.
cld.idiom:
std
rep stosw           ; bomb down
cld
rep movsw           ; copy up
cld.pitfall: A child from `spl` copies the flags of its parent, DF included.

cmc.use: Flips CF: turns "below" into "above or equal".
cmc.idiom:
cmp ax, bx
cmc                 ; CF = 1 if ax >= bx (unsigned)
cmc.pitfall: It flips CF only: ZF still says what the `cmp` said.

cmp.summary: compare: set the flags from dst - src; dst keeps its value
cmp.example:
scan: add si, 8
cmp word [si], 0
jz scan
cmp.use: Tests a value and keeps it: the scanner's `cmp word [si], 0` asks if a word is empty core.
cmp.idiom:
scan: add di, 2
cmp word [di], 0    ; empty core?
je scan             ; yes: go on
mov word [di], 0    ; no: bomb it
cmp.pitfall: The jump after it picks signed or unsigned: `jb` and `ja` compare unsigned, `jl` and `jg` compare signed. Addresses are unsigned.

cmpsb.summary: compare the byte at si with the byte at di; step si and di
cmpsb.use: Compares two runs of bytes: `repe cmpsb` finds where a copy differs from its source.
cmpsb.idiom:
mov cx, 64
repe cmpsb          ; while the bytes match
jz intact           ; all 64 match
dec si              ; si and di: the byte that differs
dec di
intact: nop
cmpsb.pitfall: The flags come from [si] - [di]. Both pointers step after the compare, so when it stops they are one past the byte that differs.

cmpsw.summary: compare the word at si with the word at di; step si and di
cmpsw.use: Compares two runs of words: a bot checks its body against a spare copy.
cmpsw.idiom:
mov cx, 16
repe cmpsw          ; 16 words, while they match
jnz hurt            ; a word differs: we were hit
jmp $
hurt: nop
cmpsw.pitfall: si and di step by 2, so they stop 2 past the word that differs.

cwd.use: Sets dx to the sign of ax before a signed divide.
cwd.idiom:
mov ax, -1000
cwd                 ; dx:ax = -1000
mov cx, 7
idiv cx             ; ax = -142, dx = -6
cwd.pitfall: Before an unsigned `div`, clear dx with `xor dx, dx`: when ax is 0x8000 or more, cwd sets dx to 0xFFFF, the quotient does not fit, and the divide kills.

dat.summary: kills the process that runs it: opcode 00, what empty core holds
dat.use: The bomb. A word of two zero bytes is a DAT, and empty core is all DAT.
dat.idiom:
jmp $
bomb: dat           ; 00 00: data after the jump, never run
dat.pitfall: Code that falls into `dat` dies (the linter warns: `dat-in-code`). `resb`, `resw`, and `align` pad with DAT too.

dec.use: Counts down. `dec word [x]` in a tight loop is an imp gate: the word changes every turn, so an imp that lands on it breaks.
dec.idiom:
gate: dec word [bx-16]  ; an imp word here changes before it runs
jmp gate
dec.pitfall: It keeps CF, like `inc`. For a counted loop, `loop` does the `dec cx` and the jump in one instruction and keeps the flags.

div.summary: unsigned divide ax (word: dx:ax) by src; a 0 divisor or an overflow kills
div.use: Divides unsigned: the remainder wraps a counter into a range.
div.idiom:
xor dx, dx          ; dx:ax = ax
mov cx, 7
div cx              ; ax = ax / 7, dx = ax mod 7
div.pitfall: A 0 divisor, or a quotient too big for ax (al for a byte), kills the process with reason `div`. dx is the high half of the dividend: clear it first.

hlt.summary: kill the process that runs it
hlt.use: Ends a process on purpose. With fewer processes, each of the rest gets more turns.
hlt.idiom:
spl worker
hlt                 ; the parent ends; the child goes on
worker: nop
hlt.pitfall: It kills: a bot whose last process runs `hlt` loses. The linter warns: `hlt-in-code`.

idiv.summary: signed divide ax (word: dx:ax) by src; a 0 divisor or an overflow kills
idiv.use: Divides signed; the quotient rounds toward 0.
idiv.idiom:
mov ax, -7
cwd
mov cx, 2
idiv cx             ; ax = -3, dx = -1
idiv.pitfall: It kills on a 0 divisor, on a quotient out of range, and on a quotient of exactly -32768 (-128 for a byte), as the 8086 does.

imul.summary: signed multiply: ax = al * src (word: dx:ax = ax * src)
imul.use: Multiplies signed values, for strides that can be negative.
imul.idiom:
mov ax, -3
mov cx, 100
imul cx             ; dx:ax = -300: dx = 0xFFFF, ax = 0xFED4
imul.pitfall: Only the 1-operand form exists: `imul ax, bx, 3` (80186) is an error. ZF SF AF PF read 0 after it, so `jz` does not test the product.

inc.use: Counts up. `inc r16` is 1 byte (`40+r`); `add r16, 1` is 3.
inc.idiom:
inc word [bx+hits]  ; count in our own data, through the base
jmp $
hits: dw 0
inc.pitfall: It keeps CF, so a `jc` after it reads an older carry. At 0xFFFF it wraps to 0 and sets ZF.

int3.summary: kill the process that runs it; debugger breakpoints never write it
int3.use: A 1-byte kill. A fill of `0xCC` kills a process that runs any byte of it, and a scan for non-zero bytes stops on it: a decoy that bites.
int3.idiom:
mov al, 0xCC
mov cx, 32
rep stosb           ; 32 bytes that kill
int3.pitfall: It kills in the arena and in the debugger alike: the debugger's breakpoints are its own and never write `CC`.

ja.summary: jump if above, unsigned: CF=0 and ZF=0
ja.example:
top: sub cx, 2
cmp cx, 8
ja top
ja.use: Unsigned above: after `cmp a, b`, jumps if a > b.
ja.idiom:
cmp ax, bx
ja keep
mov ax, bx          ; ax = the larger, unsigned
keep: nop
ja.pitfall: `ja` is unsigned; `jg` is its signed twin. For addresses, use `ja`.

jc.summary: jump if carry, or below unsigned: CF=1
jc.use: Unsigned below: after `cmp a, b`, jumps if a < b. It also reads the bit a shift pushed out.
jc.idiom:
cmp dx, 64
jc skip             ; dx < 64: inside our body
mov word [di], 0
skip: add di, 4
jc.pitfall: `jb`, `jc`, and `jnae` are one instruction. `inc` and `dec` keep CF, so a `jc` after them reads an older carry.

jcxz.summary: jump if cx is 0: guards a loop that would run 65,536 times
jcxz.example:
jcxz done
copy: movsw
loop copy
done: ret
jcxz.use: Skips a `loop` when the count is 0.
jcxz.idiom:
jcxz done
top: mov word [di], 0
add di, 8
loop top
done: nop
jcxz.pitfall: It reads cx, not the flags. There is no `jcxnz`: use `test cx, cx` and `jnz`. A `rep` needs no guard: with cx = 0 it does nothing.

jg.summary: jump if greater, signed: ZF=0 and SF=OF
jg.example:
top: dec ax
cmp ax, 10
jg top
jg.use: Signed greater: after `cmp a, b`, jumps if a > b as signed values.
jg.idiom:
cmp ax, bx
jg keep
mov ax, bx          ; ax = the larger, signed
keep: nop
jg.pitfall: `jg` is signed; `ja` is its unsigned twin.

jl.example:
top: inc ax
cmp ax, bx
jl top
jl.use: Signed less: after `cmp a, b`, jumps if a < b as signed values.
jl.idiom:
cmp ax, bx
jl keep
mov ax, bx          ; ax = the smaller, signed
keep: nop
jl.pitfall: It is signed: 0xFFFF is -1, less than 0. For addresses, use `jb`.

jmp.summary: jump to a label, or to the address in a register or memory
jmp.use: Loops and skips data. `jmp $` spins in place: a process that stays alive and does nothing.
jmp.idiom:
mov word [di], 0
jmp $               ; spin: EB FE
jmp.pitfall: `jmp label` is relative and position independent; `jmp bx` and `jmp word [x]` go to an absolute address. There is no conditional rel16 jump: to reach far, jump over a `jmp` with the inverted condition.

jna.summary: jump if not above, unsigned: CF=1 or ZF=1
jna.example:
top: add di, 2
cmp di, si
jna top
jna.use: Unsigned below or equal: one compare checks that a value is in 0..n.
jna.idiom:
cmp dx, 63
jbe skip            ; dx in 0..63: our own 64 bytes
mov word [di], 0
skip: add di, 4
jna.pitfall: It is unsigned: -1 (0xFFFF) is above 63. That is what makes one `cmp` a range check.

jnc.summary: jump if no carry, or above or equal unsigned: CF=0
jnc.use: Unsigned above or equal: after `cmp a, b`, jumps if a >= b.
jnc.idiom:
top: sub cx, 2
jnc top             ; loop until cx borrows
jnc.pitfall: `jae`, `jnb`, and `jnc` are one instruction. It is unsigned: -1 (0xFFFF) is above everything.

jng.summary: jump if not greater, signed: ZF=1 or SF≠OF
jng.example:
top: inc ax
cmp ax, 10
jng top
jng.use: Signed less or equal: guards a loop whose count may be 0 or negative.
jng.idiom:
cmp cx, 0
jng done            ; a count of 0 or less: nothing to copy
copy: movsw
loop copy
done: nop
jng.pitfall: `jle` and `jng` are one instruction. A count of 0x8000 or more is negative here.

jnl.summary: jump if not less, signed: SF=OF
jnl.example:
top: dec ax
cmp ax, bx
jnl top
jnl.use: Signed greater or equal. After `sub ax, n`, it tests the old ax against n.
jnl.idiom:
top: sub ax, 7
jnl top             ; again while ax was 7 or more
add ax, 7           ; ax = ax mod 7, for ax >= 0
jnl.pitfall: `jge` and `jnl` are one instruction. It reads SF and OF, not CF.

jno.use: Goes on while a signed value has not wrapped.
jno.idiom:
add ax, bx
jno done
mov ax, 0x7FFF      ; clamp, for ax and bx >= 0
done: nop

jns.summary: jump if not sign, 0 or positive: SF=0
jns.use: Zero or positive: bit 15 of the result is 0.
jns.idiom:
test ax, ax
jns done
neg ax              ; ax = |ax|
done: nop
jns.pitfall: Addresses 0x8000 and up read as negative: do not use `jns` to compare addresses.

jnz.summary: jump if not zero, or not equal: ZF=0
jnz.use: Loops until a count reaches 0, or jumps on not equal.
jnz.idiom:
mov cx, 8
top: mov word [di], 0
add di, 16
dec cx
jnz top             ; 8 bombs, 16 bytes apart
jnz.pitfall: `loop` does `dec cx` and the jump in one instruction; `dec` and `jnz` work with any register.

jo.example:
add ax, bx
jo clip
clip: mov ax, 0x7FFF
jo.use: Catches a signed overflow, to clamp a value. Rare in bots.
jo.idiom:
count: inc dx
add ax, 0x0800
jo done             ; stop at the first signed wrap
jmp count
done: nop
jo.pitfall: OF is signed overflow; for an unsigned one, test CF with `jc`.

jpe.summary: jump if parity even, an even count of 1 bits in the low byte: PF=1
jpe.example:
test al, al
jpe even
even: nop
jpe.use: Parity of the low byte: an even count of 1 bits. Rare in bots.
jpe.idiom:
test al, al
jpe even
xor al, 0x80        ; bit 7 as a parity bit: now even
even: nop
jpe.pitfall: PF counts the low 8 bits only, even for a word result.

jpo.summary: jump if parity odd, an odd count of 1 bits in the low byte: PF=0
jpo.example:
test al, al
jpo odd
odd: nop
jpo.use: Parity of the low byte: an odd count of 1 bits.
jpo.idiom:
and al, 3
jpo mixed           ; al is 1 or 2: one bit of the two
mov al, 0
mixed: nop
jpo.pitfall: `jnp` and `jpo` are one instruction. PF counts the low 8 bits only.

js.use: Negative: bit 15 of the result is 1.
js.idiom:
sub ax, bx
js under            ; ax < bx, as signed values that did not overflow
jmp done
under: neg ax
done: nop
js.pitfall: After a signed overflow, SF is wrong; `jl` reads SF and OF together and is right.

jz.summary: jump if zero, or equal: ZF=1
jz.example:
scan: add si, 8
cmp word [si], 0
jz scan
jz.use: Equal, or zero: after `cmp`, after `test`, or after a count reaches 0.
jz.idiom:
mov si, di
scan: add si, 16
cmp word [si], 0
je scan             ; skip empty core
jz.pitfall: `je` and `jz` are one instruction. rel8 only: the target must be within -128..+127 bytes.

lahf.summary: copy SF ZF AF PF CF into ah
lahf.use: Copies SF ZF AF PF CF into ah, so a flag becomes a value to test, store, or add.
lahf.idiom:
cmp ax, bx
lahf
and ah, 0x40        ; ah = 0x40 if ax = bx, else 0
lahf.pitfall: Bits 5, 3, and 1 of ah are 0, 0, and 1, not flags. OF is not in ah: use `pushf` for it.

lea.summary: load the address of a memory operand, not the value there
lea.use: Computes an address from a base register, with no memory access: `lea di, [bx+end]` points di just past the bot.
lea.idiom:
start: call .here
.here: pop bx
sub bx, .here
lea di, [bx+start-2]  ; di = the word just under the bot
lea.pitfall: `lea` takes a memory operand only: `lea ax, bx` is an error, and the bytes `8D` with mod = 11 kill. It changes no flags, so it cannot stand in for `add` before a `jz`.

lodsb.summary: load the byte at si into al; step si
lodsb.use: Reads the next byte at si and steps si.
lodsb.idiom:
mov cx, 8
xor dx, dx
sum: lodsb
add dl, al          ; dl = the sum of 8 bytes: a cheap checksum
loop sum
lodsb.pitfall: `rep lodsb` is legal and useless: each load overwrites al. To find a byte, use `repne scasb`.

lodsw.summary: load the word at si into ax; step si
lodsw.use: Reads the next word at si and steps si: a sampler.
lodsw.idiom:
top: lodsw
add si, 14          ; a word every 16 bytes
test ax, ax
jz top              ; skip empty core
lodsw.pitfall: si steps by 2 whatever the data; add to si for a larger stride.

loop.summary: cx -= 1, then jump if cx is not 0
loop.use: Counts a loop in one instruction: cx -= 1, and jump while cx is not 0. The dwarf counts its lap with it.
loop.idiom:
mov cx, 100
bomb: sub di, 4
mov word [di], 0
loop bomb           ; 100 bombs
loop.pitfall: With cx = 0, `loop` wraps cx to 0xFFFF and runs 65,536 times: guard it with `jcxz`. The target is rel8: at most 128 bytes back from the end of the `loop`.

loope.summary: cx -= 1, then jump if cx is not 0 and ZF=1
loope.use: Goes on while a test says equal, up to cx times.
loope.idiom:
mov cx, 64
skip: lodsw
test ax, ax
loope skip          ; pass empty words, up to 64
loope.pitfall: `loopz` and `loope` are one instruction. When cx reaches 0 it stops whatever ZF is.

loopne.summary: cx -= 1, then jump if cx is not 0 and ZF=0
loopne.use: Searches: counts and tests in one instruction, and stops on a match or at the end of the count.
loopne.idiom:
mov cx, 256
find: lodsb
cmp al, 0xE9        ; a jmp rel16 opcode?
loopne find         ; stop on it, or after 256 bytes
loopne.pitfall: It does not change the flags, so ZF comes from the instruction before it. After the loop, test ZF to tell a match from the end of the count.

mov.summary: copy a byte or word: dst = src
mov.use: Writes bombs and reads data. `mov word [di], 0` is the dwarf's bomb: two zero bytes, one DAT.
mov.idiom:
xor ax, ax          ; ax = 0, the bomb
mov [di], ax        ; 2 bytes: mov word [di], 0 is 4
mov.pitfall: `mov ax, [label]` reads the fixed address `label` of the core, not your copy of it: the loader does not relocate. Read your own data as `[bx+label]` after the base idiom.

movsb.summary: copy the byte at si to di; step si and di
movsb.use: Copies one byte and steps si and di. `rep movsb` copies an odd length exactly.
movsb.idiom:
mov cx, 33
rep movsb           ; 33 bytes, 33 cycles
movsb.pitfall: `movsw` copies twice the bytes per cycle; use `movsb` for an odd tail only.

movsw.summary: copy the word at si to di; step si and di
movsw.use: The imp's instruction and paper's copy. With di one word after si, `movsw` copies the word it runs to the next word.
movsw.idiom:
mov si, bx          ; from our base
mov di, dx
mov cx, 32
rep movsw           ; 64 bytes to dx, a word a cycle
spl dx              ; start the copy
movsw.pitfall: `rep movsw` takes one cycle per word, and an enemy can bomb the copy before it ends. After it, si and di point past the copy, not at its start.

mul.summary: unsigned multiply: ax = al * src (word: dx:ax = ax * src)
mul.use: Multiplies for a random walk: one step of a linear congruential generator (LCG).
mul.idiom:
mov cx, 25173
mul cx              ; dx:ax = ax * 25173
add ax, 13849       ; ax = the next LCG value
mul.pitfall: It writes dx (ah for a byte) even when the product is small. It takes no immediate: `mul 5` is an error.

neg.use: Turns a stride around, or a negative distance into a positive one.
neg.idiom:
neg dx              ; walk the other way
add di, dx
neg.pitfall: CF is 1 for every value but 0. `neg` of 0x8000 is 0x8000, with OF set.

nop.use: Takes a cycle and does nothing. The imp's `movsw` is 1 byte; `nop` fills its word.
nop.idiom:
imp: movsw
nop                 ; A5 90: the word the imp copies ahead
nop.pitfall: `90` is `xchg ax, ax` on the 8086; x16c writes `xchg ax, ax` as `87 C0`. A run of `90` bytes is a slide: a process runs through it into whatever comes next.

not.use: Flips every bit: 0 becomes 0xFFFF, a non-zero fill.
not.idiom:
xor ax, ax
not ax              ; ax = 0xFFFF
not.pitfall: It changes no flag: a `jz` after `not` reads the flags from before. `not` is one less than `neg`: not x = -x - 1.

or.summary: bitwise or: dst |= src; clears CF and OF
or.example:
or ax, ax
jz empty
empty: nop
or.use: Merges values. A chain of `or` tests several words for non-zero in one jump, as the vampire samples the core.
or.idiom:
mov dx, [di]
or dx, [di-16]
or dx, [di-32]      ; ZF = 0 if any of the 3 words is not empty
or.pitfall: `or ax, ax` sets the flags like `test ax, ax` but writes ax back. With a memory destination, that is a write to the core.

pop.summary: load the word at sp into dst, then sp += 2
pop.use: Reads the word at sp and moves sp up. After `call`, it gets the address of the next line: the base idiom.
pop.idiom:
start: call .here
.here: pop bx       ; bx = the address of .here
sub bx, .here       ; bx = the base of the bot
pop.pitfall: The word at sp is whatever the core holds there, enemy bombs included. `pop sp` leaves sp equal to the popped word, not that word plus 2.

popf.summary: pop a word into FLAGS: OF DF SF ZF AF PF CF
popf.use: Puts back flags that `pushf` saved, or sets several flags from a word.
popf.idiom:
pushf
std
rep movsw           ; a copy that steps down
popf                ; DF is what it was
popf.pitfall: Only OF DF SF ZF AF PF CF take bits from the word; the others are lost. A stray word on the stack can set DF, and then every string instruction runs backward.

push.summary: sp -= 2, then store the word at sp
push.use: Writes a word at sp - 2 and moves sp down: a store and a step in 1 byte. sp starts at the base, so the stack grows into the core under the bot.
push.idiom:
xor ax, ax
mov sp, di          ; aim the stack at the target
push ax             ; DAT at di-2
push ax             ; DAT at di-4
push.pitfall: `push sp` pushes sp after the decrement, as the 8086 does. `push 5` is an error: the 8086 has no `push imm`. Load a register first.

pushf.use: Saves the flags across code that changes them.
pushf.idiom:
pushf
cmp ax, bx
popf                ; the flags from before the cmp are back
pushf.pitfall: It writes 2 bytes at sp - 2 like any push: with sp at the base, the word just under the bot. Bit 1 of the word is 1, and I and T are 0.

rcl.use: Shifts CF into bit 0: carries a shift into a second word, or turns a flag into a bit.
rcl.idiom:
xor ax, ax
cmp si, di
rcl ax, 1           ; ax = 1 if si < di (unsigned), else 0
rcl.pitfall: It reads CF: a stale carry goes into bit 0. Use `clc` first when it must be 0.

rcr.use: Shifts CF into the top bit: the low word of a 32-bit right shift.
rcr.idiom:
stc
rcr ax, 1           ; bit 15 of ax is now 1
rcr.pitfall: It reads CF into bit 15. After `shr dx, 1`, CF is the bit that fell out of dx, which is what a 32-bit shift needs.

ret.summary: pop an address and jump to it; ret n then drops n more bytes
ret.use: Returns from a `call`, or jumps to any address on the stack: `push dx` then `ret` is `jmp dx`.
ret.idiom:
push dx
ret                 ; jump to the address in dx
ret.pitfall: It trusts the stack: the word at sp may be anything. `ret n` pops, then adds n to sp.

rol.summary: rotate left: the top bit goes to bit 0 and CF
rol.use: Rotates bits around with none lost: a stride that changes each pass and never becomes 0.
rol.idiom:
rol dx, 1           ; a new stride from the old one
add di, dx
rol.pitfall: The count is `1` or `cl`, and a count in cl is not masked: a word rotate by 17 is a rotate by 1, 17 steps. A count of 0 changes no flag.

ror.summary: rotate right: bit 0 goes to the top bit and CF
ror.use: Rotates right. A word rotate by 8 swaps its bytes.
ror.idiom:
mov cl, 8
ror ax, cl          ; swap al and ah
ror.pitfall: Only `1` and `cl` are counts: `ror ax, 8` is an error on the 8086. `xchg al, ah` is shorter.

sahf.summary: copy ah into SF ZF AF PF CF
sahf.use: Sets SF ZF AF PF CF from ah in one byte.
sahf.idiom:
mov ah, 0x41        ; bits 6 and 0: ZF and CF
sahf                ; ZF = 1, CF = 1, SF AF PF = 0
sahf.pitfall: It does not touch OF or DF. The bits of ah are SF ZF - AF - PF - CF from bit 7 down, so ZF is bit 6, not bit 0.

sar.summary: shift right, copies of the sign bit in: a signed halve
sar.use: Halves signed: the sign bit stays.
sar.idiom:
mov ax, -7
sar ax, 1           ; ax = -4: it rounds down
sar.pitfall: It rounds toward minus infinity, where `idiv` by 2 rounds toward 0. -1 stays -1 however far it shifts.

sbb.summary: subtract with borrow: dst -= src + CF, to chain subtracts past 16 bits
sbb.example:
sub ax, bx
sbb dx, cx
sbb.use: Subtracts past 16 bits, and turns CF into a mask: `sbb ax, ax` is 0 or 0xFFFF.
sbb.idiom:
cmp si, di
sbb ax, ax          ; ax = 0xFFFF if si < di (unsigned), else 0
sbb.pitfall: It subtracts CF as well. After `cmp` or `sub`, CF is a borrow; clear it with `clc` when the chain starts fresh.

scasb.summary: compare al with the byte at di; step di
scasb.use: The scanner's search: `repe scasb` with al = 0 runs over empty core and stops after the first non-zero byte.
scasb.idiom:
xor al, al
mov cx, 0xFFFF
repe scasb          ; stops one past the first non-zero byte
dec di              ; di = the byte found
scasb.pitfall: `repe` goes on while the byte equals al; `repne` goes on while it does not. Each byte is one cycle, so a scan across a long empty gap is slow.

scasw.summary: compare ax with the word at di; step di
scasw.use: Compares ax with a word at di and steps di: a faster scan, 2 bytes a cycle.
scasw.idiom:
xor ax, ax
mov cx, 32
repe scasw          ; pass up to 32 empty words
jnz found           ; a word was not empty
jmp $
found: nop
scasw.pitfall: It stops 2 past the word it found. One non-zero byte stops it, in either half.

shl.summary: shift left, zeros in: an unsigned double
shl.use: Doubles: `shl ax, 1` is ax * 2 in one cycle, with no `mul`.
shl.idiom:
mov ax, bx
shl ax, 1
shl ax, 1           ; ax = bx * 4
shl.pitfall: `sal` is the same instruction. Bits shifted past bit 15 are gone; CF holds the last one out.

shr.summary: shift right, zeros in: an unsigned halve
shr.use: Halves unsigned: bytes to words for a copy, or a step of a binary search.
shr.idiom:
mov cx, 34
shr cx, 1           ; 17 words in 34 bytes
rep movsw
shr.pitfall: An odd value loses its low bit. To round a byte count up to words, add 1 first: `(SIZE + 1) / 2`.

spl.summary: start a new process at the target; this one goes on to the next line
spl.example:
spl bomber
guard: jmp guard
bomber: mov word [di], 0
spl.use: Starts another process of the bot at the target. The bot still runs one instruction a cycle, shared by its processes: splitting buys survival, not speed.
spl.idiom:
spl $+2             ; 2 processes on the next line
spl $+2             ; 4
spl $+2             ; 8, each running the code below
spl.pitfall: At the process cap (64 a bot by default) `spl` does nothing. `spl label` is relative; `spl dx` goes to the absolute address in dx. The child copies all registers, so it starts with the parent's di and bx.

stc.use: Sets CF: a "yes" answer from a subroutine, or a 1 to shift in with `rcr`.
stc.pitfall: `inc` and `dec` keep CF, so it survives a counter step.

std.summary: set the direction flag: string instructions step down
std.use: Makes string instructions step down: scan or bomb toward lower addresses.
std.idiom:
std
xor ax, ax
mov cx, 16
rep stosw           ; 16 words of DAT, down from di
std.pitfall: With DF = 1, a copy starts at the last word: point si and di at the ends of the blocks, not the starts.

stosb.summary: store al at di; step di
stosb.use: Writes al at di and steps di: bytes of code one at a time, or a fill with `rep`.
stosb.idiom:
mov al, 0xEB        ; jmp short
stosb
mov al, 0xFE        ; -2
stosb               ; EB FE: jmp $, a trap that spins
stosb.pitfall: It steps di down when DF = 1. `stosw` fills twice as fast.

stosw.summary: store ax at di; step di
stosw.use: The carpet bomb: `rep stosw` with ax = 0 writes a run of DAT, a word a cycle.
stosw.idiom:
xor ax, ax
mov cx, 16
rep stosw           ; 32 bytes of DAT at di
stosw.pitfall: Point di first: registers start at 0, so a bot that never sets di bombs from address 0 (the linter warns: `uninitialized-di`).

sub.use: Steps down, and turns an address into a distance: `sub bx, .here` in the base idiom, and `sub dx, bx` to find a hit relative to the base.
sub.idiom:
sub dx, bx          ; dx = hit - base
cmp dx, 64          ; our body is 64 bytes
jb skip             ; one unsigned compare: under 64 is us
mov word [di], 0
skip: add di, 2
sub.pitfall: `sub` changes CF and `dec` does not. A distance under the base wraps to a large number: that is why one unsigned `cmp` checks both ends of a range.

test.summary: and without storing: set the flags from dst & src
test.use: Checks bits and writes nothing: `test ax, ax` then `jz` asks if ax is 0.
test.idiom:
test al, 1
jz even             ; bit 0 is 0
inc al              ; make al even
even: nop
test.pitfall: `test al, 1` then `jz` jumps when the bit is 0, not when it is 1. It sets CF and OF to 0.

xchg.use: Swaps two values in one instruction, with no scratch register. Paper swaps the bytes of its base to start its path far away.
xchg.idiom:
mov dx, bx
xchg dl, dh         ; our base, bytes swapped: a far-away address
xchg.pitfall: `xchg` with a memory operand writes that memory: `xchg ax, [si]` to read a word also stores ax there. `xchg ax, ax` assembles to `87 C0`, because `90` is `nop`.

xor.summary: bitwise xor: dst ^= src; clears CF and OF
xor.use: `xor ax, ax` zeros a register in 2 bytes: the usual bomb value.
xor.idiom:
xor ax, ax          ; ax = 0
mov [di], ax        ; a DAT bomb
xor.pitfall: `xor ax, ax` also sets ZF and clears CF; `mov ax, 0` keeps the flags. Between a `cmp` and its jump, use mov.

rep.summary: repeat a string instruction while cx is not 0, cx -= 1 each time, one a cycle
rep.use: Repeats `movs`, `stos`, or `lods` cx times, one iteration a cycle: the copy and the carpet.
rep.idiom:
xor ax, ax
mov cx, 64
rep stosw           ; 128 bytes of DAT in 64 cycles
rep.pitfall: Between iterations, ip stays on the prefix: a bomb there ends the copy and the process. With cx = 0, it takes one cycle and does nothing. `rep` and `repe` are one byte, `F3`: on `cmps` and `scas`, `rep` repeats while equal.

repe.summary: repeat cmps or scas while cx is not 0 and ZF=1 (equal), one a cycle
repe.use: Repeats `cmps` or `scas` while the values are equal: with al = 0, `repe scasb` passes over empty core.
repe.idiom:
xor al, al
mov cx, 512
repe scasb          ; stops after a non-zero byte, or after 512
repe.pitfall: It also stops when cx reaches 0. Test ZF after it to tell a hit from the end of the count.

repne.summary: repeat cmps or scas while cx is not 0 and ZF=0 (not equal), one a cycle
repne.use: Repeats `cmps` or `scas` while the values differ: finds a given byte or word.
repne.idiom:
mov al, 0xE9        ; a jmp rel16 opcode
mov cx, 512
repne scasb         ; stops one past it, or after 512
repne.pitfall: di stops one past the match (two for `scasw`). `repnz` and `repne` are one prefix.
